source.title: Sapiens: Foundation for Human Vision Models
source.authors: Rawal Khirodkar; Timur M. Bagautdinov; Julieta Martinez; Zhao-En Su; A. James; Peter Selednik; Stuart Anderson; Shunsuke Saito

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends model-scaling evaluations to vision models and downstream human-vision tasks. It reports performance across model sizes, but does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Rows record the reported downstream benchmark metrics across Sapiens parameter sizes and the normal-estimation data-size sweep in Figure 10. The paper does not measure language-model pretraining loss, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Table 7 compares pretraining sources and is not a clean scale sweep. Other reported metrics are left out where they do not meet the rule for adding secondary metrics.
record.test_reason: Sapiens is a vision model release, not a test of any version. Its scale results are fine-tuned human-vision task metrics for MAE-pretrained ViT encoders at four sizes (0.3B–2B), plus one 1M–50M pretraining-image sweep. The paper fits no power law and checks no extrapolation, compute-optimal split or loss–downstream link. The claim concerns language models. V5 needs the power-law form to be shown in another modality, and V6 needs predictable improvement, which four unfitted points cannot show. The size sweep is also confounded: batch size varies from 98,304 to 20,480, and every model sees 1.2T tokens regardless of size. The monotonic gains are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors attribute their state-of-the-art results to human-centric curated pretraining, high-resolution high-capacity backbones and high-quality annotations. They report that performance improves with model size (0.3B→2B) and with more unique pretraining images. They make no scaling-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: Uses masked-autoencoder pretraining of vision transformers on human images, followed by task-specific fine-tuning and downstream vision metrics; it does not measure language-model loss or use the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Task metrics and evaluation datasets differ across pose, segmentation, depth, and surface-normal experiments; Figure 10 varies the number of unique human images seen during pretraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned downstream metrics for pose, segmentation, depth and normals improve almost monotonically as MAE ViT encoder size goes from 0.3B to 2B. There are ties at 0.3B/0.6B on depth and a flat 1B→2B step on Hi4D normals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream human-vision task performance of MAE-pretrained ViTs improves monotonically with encoder size (no functional form established).

fits_no_version.finding: For Sapiens-0.3B, normal-estimation accuracy (% within 30°) rises from 40.5 to 66.1 as unique pretraining images go from 1M to 50M, with no saturation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of vision MAE models increases with the number of unique pretraining images at fixed model size.

record.problems: The Sapiens size sweep covers four models (0.336 B to 2.163 B) and reports task metrics rather than fitted or validated predictions. The study concerns vision models, not language-model loss, and reports no uncertainty for these scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: Secondary metrics and category-specific pose results in Tables 3-6 were not added because the extraction rules limit additional metrics under the same condition unless they disagree with or are compared against the primary metric. Table 7's pretraining-source comparisons were not included because they are not a clean scale sweep.

untested.parts: No language models and no held-out pretraining loss versus size; MAE reconstruction loss is not reported across sizes.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No fixed-compute allocation; every size is trained on 1.2T tokens.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count; models are scaled mainly by width, following prior work.
Vision setting, but no power-law form is fitted for loss or task metrics versus parameters or data.
No predictive relationship is fitted or validated, and downstream metrics are not related to pretraining loss. Only four sizes are tested, with batch size confounded.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label covering all 38 rows is dropped. The rows are vision task metrics from four confounded model sizes, and the paper neither fits nor tests predictability. Table 7 (data source comparison) is correctly left out as a non-scale comparison. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model pretraining loss are evaluated.
No loss laws are fitted on small runs or used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is tested.
Architecture details are not varied independently at fixed parameter count.
The paper evaluates vision models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in vision or other modalities or training regimes.

Reports downstream task metrics across four Sapiens parameter sizes and one pretraining-image-count sweep, but does not fit a predictive relationship, evaluate predictions, or relate downstream metrics to pretraining loss.
No alternative fitting choices, exponents, or curve bends are evaluated.

rows.subject: Sapiens-0.3B
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained on Humans-300M and fine-tuned for pose estimation
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated whole-body pose performance across Sapiens model sizes
rows.note: The paper reports increasing whole-body AP across the four Sapiens sizes.
rows.check: Table 3 whole-body AP rises 53.4→61.1 across sizes. The bracketed +0.3…+7.6 are gains over the prior state of the art (DWPose-l, 53.1), not over a scale baseline. These are fine-tuned vision metrics with no fitted law, so they do not measure V6 for language models.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Sapiens downstream task benchmarks across model sizes and the normal-estimation pretraining-image sweep
reader_labels.reason: Reported downstream scores improve across the Sapiens sizes, and the normal-estimation score rises with more unique pretraining images (R1-R38); the study does not fit or validate a predictive law.
